before.title: Real heights keep extended-real convexity precise
before.summary: These are the library proof routes for the selected definitions, domain and indicator consequences, Theorem 2.4 and Examples 2.5–2.6. Orabona cites Rockafellar for Theorem 2.4 and leaves the norm example as an exercise.

steps.title: Project the epigraph to the effective domain
steps.detail: Every value below positive infinity has a real upper bound, even when the value is negative infinity. Lift two domain points to real epigraph heights. Convexity combines these lifts; the resulting finite height witnesses domain membership.
steps.fallback: Domain points admit real epigraph heights; their convex combinations do too.

steps.title: Use real values only where finiteness is proved
steps.detail: For Theorem 2.4, the no-negative-infinity hypothesis and domain membership prove that each value is finite. Convexity of the effective domain proves this also for the interpolated point. The real epigraph equivalence then translates the ordinary convexity inequality in both directions. Infinite values are never globally identified with zero.
steps.fallback: Under no-bottom and a convex effective domain, the strict-weight inequality is equivalent to epigraph convexity.

steps.title: Read constraints as epigraph intersections
steps.detail: The indicator epigraph is the product of the feasible set and nonnegative real heights. Adding an indicator intersects the original epigraph with the feasible cylinder; the no-bottom assumption excludes ambiguous infinite addition. Convexity follows from products and intersections of convex sets.
steps.fallback: Indicator convexity is equivalent to convexity of V; adding it restricts the epigraph to V.

steps.title: Check the affine and norm examples
steps.detail: Affine evaluation preserves convex combinations exactly. For the norm, apply the triangle inequality followed by nonnegative homogeneity. The real-valued coercion bridge transfers these inequalities into the same extended-real epigraph definition.
steps.fallback: Affine functions satisfy equality; the norm satisfies the convexity inequality.

before.boundary: Abstract real modules and normed spaces generalize the printed Euclidean examples. Empty domains are permitted. No-bottom is required only where stated. steps.title: Separate finite loss from the below-top domain
steps.detail: Inside V the indicator is zero. Outside V it is top: adding bottom gives bottom, and adding a finite value or top gives top, never a finite real. Thus a finite constrained value requires both feasibility and a finite original value. The separate domain identity excludes bottom globally, so outside V the sum is top.
steps.math: \(f(x)+\iota_V(x)\in\mathbb R\iff x\in V\ \land\ f(x)\in\mathbb R;\qquad f> -\infty\Rightarrow\operatorname{dom}(f+\iota_V)=\operatorname{dom}f\cap V.\)
steps.fallback: Finite values exclude both infinities; the below-top domain excludes only positive infinity.

after.title: Feasible directions characterize a constrained minimum
after.summary: These are the retained library proof steps. The source attribution and the explicit generalization of neighborhood convexity are stated above. The source proves the interior implication by a small displacement opposite the gradient; this implementation instead applies local-minimum Fermat after proving ambient local minimality.

steps.title: Transfer finite values without changing order
steps.detail: Put F(z)=(f(z)).toReal. F embeds back to f on the finite open neighborhood U, hence on V. Rewrite both compared values at x and y to transfer minimum inequalities. This order helper needs finiteness only on V and explicit x membership; its ambient complete-inner-product context is retained.
steps.fallback: Finite coercions preserve each comparison on V.

steps.title: Differentiate along a feasible segment
steps.detail: A constrained minimum on convex V has nonnegative derivative along y-x for every feasible y. The actual derivative at x is supplied by differentiability on open U. The real helper uses the positive tangent cone of the segment.
steps.fallback: A feasible segment cannot initially decrease from a minimum.

steps.title: Use the supporting inequality for sufficiency
steps.detail: Convexity on V gives the previously proved gradient lower bound. If every feasible inner product is nonnegative, the bound proves F(y) at least F(x), and finite coercion gives the original minimum.
steps.fallback: The supporting plane turns the directional condition into a global minimum on V.

steps.title: Add ambient interior for zero gradient
steps.detail: At an ambient-interior point, the constrained minimum is an ambient local minimum, so Fermat gives zero gradient. Conversely, zero gradient satisfies every feasible directional inequality. A boundary point need not have zero gradient.
steps.fallback: Only the interior consequence identifies minima with zero gradient.

after.title: Reach the original convex set
after.summary: This is the library induction used by Jensen. The target is membership in the possibly nonclosed set itself.

steps.title: Begin with closure membership
steps.detail: Closed-convex integral theory places the mean m in closure s. If m were absent from s, it could not lie in its ambient interior.
steps.fallback: Closure membership starts the argument but does not finish it.

steps.title: Produce a nonzero support
steps.detail: For nonempty ambient interior use geometric separation; otherwise annihilate the proper affine-span direction. Either route gives a nonzero continuous linear functional supporting s at m. These are alternative geometric cases.
steps.fallback: Separation or a proper affine span supplies the supporting functional.

steps.title: Turn the inequality into almost-sure equality
steps.detail: Linear integral commutation and probability mass one make the integrals of a(X) and the constant a(m) equal. Together with the almost-sure inequality and integrability this forces equality of these scalar values almost everywhere.
steps.fallback: The functional values agree almost surely; X need not be constant.

steps.title: Descend into the proper kernel
steps.detail: Center X at m and lift it into K=ker a almost everywhere, using zero only on the null exceptional set. The subtype isometry proves integrability and linear integral commutation proves mean zero. The affine preimage of s is convex and contains the lift almost surely. Its dimension is strictly smaller, so strong induction puts zero in that preimage and therefore m in s.
steps.math: \(K=\ker a,\quad\dim K<\dim E,\quad Y=X-m\text{ a.e.},\quad\int Y\,d\mu=0,\quad 0\in\{v\in K:v+m\in s\}.\)
steps.fallback: A lower-dimensional convex-set statement proves the original membership.

after.boundary: Finite dimension, probability mass one, genuine integrability and almost-sure set membership are retained. Closedness, nonempty ambient interior and finite support are not assumed. The scalar support-equality helper allows a zero functional; the geometric step produces a nonzero one for rank descent.

steps.title: Support a finite epigraph boundary
steps.detail: If f is finite throughout a neighborhood of x, the point (x,f(x)) lies on the boundary of the real-height epigraph. A nonzero separating functional splits as L(y,t)=A(y)+ct. Upward epigraph closure gives c at most zero. If c were zero, A would have a local maximum and hence be zero; this contradicts the nonzero separator.
steps.fallback: Neighborhood finiteness excludes a vertical supporting hyperplane.

steps.title: Normalize only after proving the sign
steps.detail: The negative coefficient also excludes a bottom value anywhere: arbitrary real heights above a bottom value contradict the support inequality. Division by c then gives a global affine lower bound touching f at x. No derivative of f is assumed; Fermat is used only on auxiliary identity and linear functions.
steps.fallback: The sign proof justifies division and produces the affine support.

steps.title: Find interior in the affine span
steps.detail: For a nowhere-bottom convex function with nonempty effective domain, finite-dimensional convexity supplies an intrinsic-interior point. Translate the affine span to its direction space and restrict f there. The restricted domain has ambient interior, so the preceding support construction supplies a minorant in that space.
steps.fallback: Relative geometry handles lower-dimensional domains.

steps.title: Extend and correct the intercept
steps.detail: Extend the restricted linear functional to the ambient finite-dimensional space, where it is continuous. Correct its intercept by subtracting its value at p. Domain points are represented as p+v; outside the domain the upper value is positive infinity, so the bound holds there too.
steps.fallback: Linear extension and the intercept correction give the global bound.

after.title: Produce the expectation bound in two cases
after.summary: These are the retained library steps for the displayed source inequality. The input has genuine finite Lebesgue coordinate means, represented by Bochner integrability in finite dimension. The inspected source prints no Jensen proof or extended-expectation well-definedness argument; the library steps below supply those obligations.

steps.title: Produce a finite negative part
steps.detail: Probability mass one and almost-sure domain membership give a nonempty-domain witness. Apply the global affine-minorant theorem to obtain a(X)+b, integrable because X is integrable. Its negative part bounds the negative loss part, proving the latter finite.
steps.fallback: The proof derives finite negative part; it is not an additional premise.

steps.title: Separate the positive-infinite case
steps.detail: If the positive loss integral is infinite, the finite negative part makes the signed expectation positive infinity. The desired inequality then follows from the top element. This branch does not separately assert finite expected loss.
steps.fallback: Infinite positive loss is allowed after controlling the negative part.

steps.title: Prove integrability in the finite case
steps.detail: Otherwise set Y=toReal(f(X)). Measurability and almost-sure domain membership, together with no bottom, give an exact finite embedding almost everywhere. The finite positive and negative part integrals make their maxima integrable; subtracting them proves Y integrable.
steps.fallback: Loss integrability is obtained inside this case, rather than assumed globally.

steps.title: Take the mean in the original epigraph
steps.detail: The integrable pair (X,Y) lies almost surely in the convex real-height epigraph. The finite-dimensional barycenter theorem places its mean in that same possibly nonclosed epigraph. The pair-integral identity and signed-real compatibility identify the resulting height with the expected loss.
steps.math: \((\mathbb EX,\mathbb EY)\in\operatorname{epi}_{\mathbb R}f\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(\mathbb EX)\le\mathbb EY=S_\mu(f\circ X).\)
steps.fallback: Actual epigraph membership gives the finite-case inequality.
